DR. ALES HRDLICKA SITES ARTICAN AS A DISTINCT TYPE.

Dr. Ales Hrdlicka, anthropologist of the Smithsonian Institution, claims that an American type of man is developing in the old American stock and the type has already reached a point where it is possible to distinguish it from the peoples of other countries. Dr. Hrdlicka bases this claim on fourteen years of study in which time he studied over 1500 adults. He paid special attention to those whose ancestors have been in the U. S. for 7 generations. The tall, rather narrow face of the old type has been modified with the immigrant and the result is a tall, vigorous and brainy man.

By application of his newly discovered invisible rays, that are produced by electricity, Dr. Richard Schleusner, of Patterson, N. J. has successfully restored youth to two sixtyxx year old men by the means of direct stimulation of the pituitular Gland; no surgical operation being necessary. The new rays, which are similar to X rays, but which cannot be rendered visible, were discovered some two years ago by Dz. Schleusner. They are produced by electricity, and, peculiarly, can be directed and centered on any organ within the body, without any intervening tissues or cells being as effected by them in any way. The penetrating power of these rays may be regulated by the operator. The two men to whom youth was restored, are at present thirty-five years of age, physically. They were subject to a shower of these raus, ten minutes each day continuously for three months. The rays were directed at the Pititular Gland, (which because of its position at the base and within the brain, was considered by Science impossible to stimulate). This gland is considered the main spring of youth and old age in men, the rays forced the gland to greater activity and cleared away the deposits of senility and replaced them with youth. A year after the experiment was made a test was taken and these men proved to be in the same physical condition as they were at the end of the successful experiment.

Nearly two years ago The Daily Telegraph was the first to announce that the original warrant whereby six baronets and seven esquires clapped John Bunyan in Bedford Gaol, was to be sold at public auction. When it appeared it fetched £305. The news now comes that the "wicked tinker's" anvil has been discovered, and it will forthwith be offered to collectors at Sotheby's. There seems to be no doubt about the genuinely of the find. It is in the shape of an inverted obelisk or cone, weighing about 60lb, and is 2ft in length. Stamped on its iron surface are the roughly seared words, "J. Bunyan, Hel'stow," and the date "1647." At that time Bunyan would be nineteen years of age, and would have returned home after seeing some months' active service with Fairfax. The relic was found in the following manner: An ironmonger at St. Neots, in succeeding to an old business of one Carrington, turned out and sold a large quantity of iron implements and tools as old scrap iron. A marine store dealer bought some of the rubbish, and the anvil was amongst it. St. Neots is only a few miles from Elstow—Bunyan's birthplace—which was formerly called Helenstow. When Bunyan was dreaming dreams and claiming the rights and gifts of a seer, he was exhorted by one of his more lenient judges to stick to his trade of tinker, as his "real gift lay in ye repaying of olde kettles." Fortunately for English literature, Bunyan persisted in his mission. The anvil has endured, and probably will endure, much longer than the copies of the first edition of "The Pilgrim's Progress," but what its value may be must be left to the arbitrament of auction. Four years ago one of the few copies extant of the earliest imprint of "The Pilgrim's Progress" fetched £1,475.

The electrified body of what is believed to have been an Indian or a Mound Builder has been found in the bank of a small creek at Cincinnati, Ohio by a boy, Duncan Pfau. The figure is of a lime-stone formation with the head, elbows, legs and hips, missing and the stone body is pitted and worn by weather or the stream but is strikingly life like nevertheless. The hands show wrinkles around the knuckles and most of the finger nails are clearly visible. Pectoral muscles, shoulders and ribs also are discernible. It was at first believed to be a piece of sculpture but geologists and chemists have proven beyond doubt that the object was at one time a human being. It was found on the bank of the Mill Creek where the stream had cut it out of the earth bank at a depth of 15 feet below the surface of surrounding land. During the eclipse wave a unique opportunity to study 'what happens to radio signals when the station sending them out or the observer who is listening to them is suddenly plunged into darkness by the rapidly advancing shadow of the moon on the earth. Once every few hundred years listeners in New York City suddenly have night conditions for something less than fifteen minutes time as the eclipse sweeps over them.

It is believed that valuable information on the transmission of signals through darkened air as well as information on the reflection of signals from the edge of the eclipse shadow band can be secured and from this, it may be possible to deduce whether radio waves can travel along the ground, through the sky, or along both paths. It is not desirable to depend on the ear of the observer for accurate measurement; so that automatic recorders, driven electrically are provided whereby the strength of the radio signal is recorded from moment to moment in the form of a wavevector ink line. Two complete Radicola Super-Heterodyne receivers are provided, each connected to its recorder. One will receive a signal from Schenectady, WGV, on the usual broadcasting length of 380 meters. The reason for recording a short wave is because, this will be reflected more strongly by the shadow wall of the eclipse, in all porbability, and thereby show interesting effects.
An electrical clock is provided, and both recorders are slactically wound and kept in time with the clock, the paper t tape of the recorder moving forward about one inch per minute.

The 'temperature, air pressure, and humidity will also be recorded, using a suitable thermometer, barometer and hygrometer in order that all the circumstances which might have a possible effect on the radio signals will be on the record.

Gernsback, at the right, demonstrates the instrument to a person of normal hearing. In order to hear with the Osphone, the normal person must close his ears tightly. Gernsback is using an ordinary telephone transmitter connected with a 6 volt battery to the Osphone.

HEARING THROUGH THE TEETH.
(The Osophone)

How the Osophone, the latest invention of Mr. H. Gernsback of New York, Editor of Science and Invention and Radio News, is used. This photograph shows the inventor using it in connection with a radio outfit. The Osophone (Os: bone - phone: voice) makes it possible for the hard of hearing to enjoy radio concerts and other sounds. The sound is conducted from the Osophone to the teeth and bony structure of the head to the auditory nerve. If this nerve functions at all, the Osophone will partly restore the hearing, although deaf people will derive no benefit from this new invention. Mr. Gernsback, however, has demonstrated that totally deaf people, when using this instrument, translate the vibrations imparted to their teeth, into a new sensation. This, of course, is not sound but after a totally deaf person has used the instrument for a number of weeks, he will be able to translate the meaning of the various vibrations and the rythm. In this respect, the Osophone works similar to the deaf person whose finger tip touches a telephone diaphragm. Some deaf people can translate such vibrations into a sensation that corresponds to sound.

TAKES NOISE FROM RADIO SET

One of the most important theories pertaining to radio since the vacuum tube was developed by DeForrest is the new conception of the effect of radio waves upon each other. This has been been brought out by Carl Pfansteil, radio engineer, of Waukegan, Ill. The greatest bugaboc in radio reception has been forced oscillation of the tubos, especially when receiving at long distances. In order to overcome this, Pfansteil has developed a coil that entirely eliminates the magnetic coupling which he claims causes the oscillations or whistling, thus bringing the received signal in undistorted and clearly. According to theory, the electrostatic effects scattered throughout a radio set are caused by incorrect placing of insulating materials, as well as the position of the metal parts, but by using the new coils and placing them so that the magnetic fields are at zero, all the familiar howls are done away with.

Photo shows Mr. Pfansteil at work in his laboratory on one of the sets; used using this theory. To the right of the set is an oscillator and wavemote which he uses in testing the operation of the circuit.
